pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 12–13 years

- **Topic:** Aerobic Respiration

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS3 Biology, Cellular respiration):** statutory — "aerobic and anaerobic respiration in living organisms, including the breakdown of organic molecules to enable all the other chemical processes necessary for life; a word summary for aerobic respiration".

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** MS-LS1-7 — "[curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-LS1-7]"; secondary DCI PS3.D (verbatim): "Cellular respiration in plants and animals involve chemical reactions with oxygen that release stored energy. In these processes, complex molecules containing carbon react with oxygen to produce carbon dioxide and other materials." Strong UK/US alignment.

- **Operational details:** Two ideas carry the topic. (1) Aerobic respiration RELEASES energy from glucose using oxygen, producing carbon dioxide and water — word equation: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water (+ energy released). It happens in EVERY living cell, specifically in the mitochondria, all the time — not just during exercise. (2) The single most important distinction: respiration is NOT breathing. Breathing (ventilation) is the muscular movement of air in and out of the lungs; respiration is the chemical release of energy inside cells. Breathing and heart rate rise during exercise precisely to supply more oxygen and glucose to — and remove more CO2 from — respiring muscle cells. Note 'energy released' rather than 'energy made' (energy is not created). Keep the mitochondria link concrete (ties back to the cell-parts topic) and keep the equation as a word summary, not a balanced symbol equation, at KS3.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B–C (early-formal / quantitative-adjacent). The child writes and explains the word equation, states respiration occurs in mitochondria in all cells, explains WHY exercise raises breathing/heart rate (oxygen and glucose supply, CO2 removal), and clearly separates respiration from breathing. Not yet expected: ATP, balanced symbol equation, or the biochemical stages.
bestPractices: Attack the respiration≠breathing confusion head-on and early — it is the defining misconception and everything else depends on separating the cellular chemistry from lung ventilation.
Insist respiration happens in EVERY cell ALL the time (in mitochondria), not only during exercise — exercise just increases the rate.
Teach the word equation as a story of transfer: glucose + oxygen go in, energy is RELEASED (not made), CO2 and water come out; check pupils say 'released', not 'created'.
Use the exercise link as the motivating phenomenon — measure pulse/breathing before and after activity and explain it as the body ramping up supply to respiring cells.
Anchor the location to the mitochondria the pupils met in the cell-parts topic, closing the loop between structure and function.
keyRepresentations: The word equation: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water (+ energy released)
A cell/mitochondrion 'engine' taking in glucose and oxygen and releasing energy plus CO2 and water
A supply-chain diagram: lungs→blood→cells (oxygen and glucose IN) and the reverse for CO2, distinguishing breathing from respiration
Before/after-exercise pulse and breathing-rate data linked to increased demand
commonMisconceptions: Believing respiration IS breathing — conflating cellular energy release with lung ventilation.
Thinking respiration only happens during exercise or only in the lungs — it occurs constantly in every cell's mitochondria.
Saying respiration 'makes' or 'creates' energy — energy is released/transferred from glucose, not created.
Thinking plants don't respire (only photosynthesise) — all living cells, including plant cells, respire all the time.
Assuming the purpose of breathing faster is to 'get rid of tiredness' rather than to supply more oxygen and remove more CO2 for respiration.

learn.summary: Aerobic respiration for ages 12–13: respiration releases energy from glucose using oxygen, mainly in the mitochondria of living plant and animal cells, ALL the time (not only during exercise), producing carbon dioxide and water — word summary: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water (+ energy released). The defining goal is to separate respiration (the chemical release of energy inside cells) from breathing/ventilation (the muscular movement of air in and out of the lungs), and to explain why breathing and heart rate rise during exercise: faster breathing brings in more oxygen and removes more CO2, and a faster heart rate delivers more oxygen and glucose to, and carries more CO2 away from, respiring muscle cells. Keep it as a word summary, not a balanced symbol equation; do not yet require ATP or biochemical stages. Activities below include a driveable supply model, a consolidation and recognition check, a tap-to-reveal supply-chain image, a Socratic exchange, and a predict–observe–explain investigation with germinating vs boiled peas.

activities.title: Power a runner from the inside: driveable cell-and-body model
feedback: If the learner only speeds breathing but ignores the cell, point to the labelled boundary: pumping the lungs faster is breathing — where is the energy actually released?
If the energy gauge drops, prompt: supply has fallen behind the mitochondria's demand — what two inputs do the cells need more of?
When the figure stands still, highlight that the mitochondria are still consuming glucose and oxygen: respiration has not switched off.
Confirm the word equation only once the outputs (CO2 and water) and the released energy are correctly traced from the flows; check the learner says energy is 'released', not 'made' or 'created'.
activities.rationale: NGSS MS-LS1-7 asks for a model of how matter and energy move through an organism; a two-level driveable model is proposed to make the 'every cell, all the time' point and the respiration≠breathing boundary visible and manipulable, grounding the word summary in a process the learner has driven. The ramp-up-with-demand mechanism (sliders, energy gauge, visible flows) is an optional interaction example, not a required product, and its comparative efficacy is untested.
sourceClaims: NGSS PS3.D (secondary DCI for MS-LS1-7): 'Cellular respiration in plants and animals involve chemical reactions with oxygen that release stored energy. In these processes, complex molecules containing carbon react with oxygen to produce carbon dioxide and other materials.'
learnerActions: Set an on-screen figure to rest or sprint and watch the zoomed-in muscle cell and its mitochondria below.
On 'sprint', raise breathing rate and heart rate (via sliders/controls) to keep oxygen and glucose flowing down the supply chain to the mitochondria.
Watch the mitochondrion 'engine' consume glucose and oxygen and release energy (shown as the legs doing work), plus CO2 and water as outputs.
Deliberately let supply fall behind demand and observe the energy gauge sag and the runner flag; then restore supply.

Read the labelled boundary that stays on screen: 'breathing = air in/out of lungs; respiration = this reaction in the cell', and note the reaction keeps running even when the figure just stands still.
Assemble the word equation from the glucose and oxygen flowing in and the CO2 and water flowing out.
activities.intendedInsight: Breathing (moving air at the lungs) and respiration (energy released by a reaction in the mitochondria) are different processes; respiration runs in every cell all the time, and exercise raises its rate so breathing/heart rate must rise to supply oxygen and glucose and remove CO2.

activities.title: Consolidate and check the key facts and misconception
feedback: For a 'breathing vs respiration' item, confirm by reference to location and mechanism: air movement at the lungs = breathing; energy-releasing reaction in the cell = respiration.
If a learner picks 'energy created', restate: respiration releases stored chemical energy from glucose; energy is not created from nothing.
If a learner says only animals respire, note that plant cells respire too — plants both photosynthesise (in cells with chloroplasts) AND respire (in all their living cells).
activities.rationale: These facts are crisply assessable, so a short recognition/recall set consolidates and checks the core knowledge and the central misconception. This format mainly confirms recall and recognition and does not by itself elicit the dynamic supply reasoning; pair it with a construction or investigation task.
learnerActions: Complete a fill-in-the-blank of the word equation: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water (+ energy released).
Decide for several short scenarios whether each describes breathing or respiration, and justify the choice.
Answer items on 'energy is released, not created' and 'all living cells respire, including plant cells'.
activities.intendedInsight: The word equation, the location (mitochondria), and the respiration-vs-breathing distinction are crisp, checkable facts the learner can state independently.

activities.title: Tap-to-reveal supply chain: lungs → blood → cell → mitochondrion
feedback: When the learner contrasts the two flaps, confirm the mechanism: the lungs move air; the mitochondrion runs the energy-releasing reaction.

If the learner expects the chain to change with activity, note that this static image shows the players and relationships but does not animate the ramp-up with demand — use the driveable model for that.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal image clearly presents the components, the supply relationship and the equation, and the lift-the-flap contrast makes the key distinction concrete. Its stated limit is that a static layout does not show the dynamic ramp-up with increasing demand.
learnerActions: Tap each stage of a lungs-to-cell chain to reveal what is happening there.
Lift the flap on the lungs vs the mitochondrion to contrast 'breathing happens here' with 'respiration happens here'.
Reveal the word equation at the cell, tracing oxygen and glucose IN and CO2 and water out.
activities.intendedInsight: The players (lungs, blood, cell, mitochondrion) and the equation can be laid out explicitly, and the lungs-vs-mitochondrion contrast directly addresses the breathing/respiration confusion.

activities.title: Socratic exchange with an exercise physiologist
feedback: If the learner says breathing provides the energy, redirect: breathing moves air — where is the energy-releasing reaction, and what do the muscle cells need more of?

Accept the answer once the learner locates energy release in the cell/mitochondria and frames faster breathing as bringing in more oxygen and removing CO2, and faster heart rate as delivering oxygen and glucose to the cells in the blood.
activities.rationale: A guided dialogue can prompt the learner to state and repair the misconception in their own words. It does not display the matter/energy flows, so pair it with the model or supply-chain image when the visible mechanism matters.
learnerActions: Respond in role to an exercise physiologist asking 'Why are you panting after a sprint? Where does the energy actually come from?'
When tempted to say 'breathing gives energy', answer the follow-up: where does the reaction actually happen, and what is breathing for?

Reach the conclusion that extra breathing brings in more oxygen and removes more CO2, while a faster heart rate carries oxygen and glucose to respiring cells (and CO2 away), where the energy is released.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating the reasoning out loud surfaces and corrects the breathing/respiration muddle through the learner's own explanation.

activities.title: Predict–observe–explain: germinating vs boiled peas
feedback: A prediction of 'no change' because nothing is exercising or breathing signals the exercise/breathing misconception — revisit that respiration is continuous and cellular.
If the learner is surprised the living peas warm, connect the warming to energy released by respiration in the peas' living cells.

Probe extensions: Does a potato in a dark cupboard respire, and how could you tell? Does a plant respire? If a person held their breath for a while, do their cells stop respiring immediately, or is something else going on?
activities.rationale: This predict-then-observe design makes the pre-observation reason diagnostic: the learner's stated 'why' reveals whether they think respiration needs exercise or breathing, and any warming of the living peas compared with the control provides evidence that respiration is continuous in living cells. Boiled (dead), disinfected peas act as the control, so warming from microbes or from the setup itself can be ruled out.
learnerActions: Set up two vacuum flasks, each with a temperature probe and loosely plugged with cotton wool so air can get in: one with living germinating peas, one with peas that were boiled (dead) then cooled. Rinse both batches in dilute disinfectant first so microbes on the peas cannot respire and warm either flask.
BEFORE observing, predict which flask (if either) will warm up over a day, and explain WHY.
Over the day, record the temperatures and compare them with the prediction.

Explain the result: if the living peas warm while the boiled peas do not, that is evidence that respiration releases energy (some of it as heat) even in still organisms that do not breathe; relate this to 'every living cell, all the time'.
activities.intendedInsight: Respiration releases energy continuously in living cells, independent of breathing or exercise — a resting organism with no lungs or ventilation (germinating peas) is expected to warm because its cells respire, while the disinfected boiled-pea control should not.

constraints: Keep the equation as a word summary (glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy released), not a balanced symbol equation, at this level.
Do not yet require ATP, the balanced symbol equation, or the biochemical stages.
Always use 'energy released'/'transferred', never 'energy made' or 'created' — energy is not created.
Anchor the location to the mitochondria met in the earlier cell-parts topic, linking structure to function.

The recognition/recall check mainly confirms facts and the misconception; it does not by itself elicit independent construction of the supply reasoning — pair it with the model, dialogue, or investigation.
The static supply-chain image shows players and relationships but does not animate the ramp-up with demand; use the driveable model when the dynamic mechanism matters.
The Socratic dialogue surfaces and repairs reasoning but does not display the matter/energy flows.

In the pea investigation, use proper safety when boiling. Plug the vacuum flasks loosely with cotton wool rather than sealing them airtight, so the living peas keep getting oxygen. Rinse both batches of peas in dilute disinfectant so microbes do not respire and warm the dead control. The boiled peas are the dead control and must be cooled before going into the flask.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source rated a 3D interactive as 'poor' because the concept is chemical/supply rather than spatial. This is a catalog-fit judgement, not an established pedagogical law, so it is omitted rather than asserted as '3D adds nothing'; a 2D model is proposed on the stated affordance that it makes the flows and boundary manipulable.

The source's claim that the driveable model is the only way to make the distinction 'felt' is a design preference, not established comparative efficacy; multiple activities (image, dialogue, investigation) are retained as genuine alternatives.
One error-pattern entry referenced a reteach prerequisite id (mt_V9SQS9gLFw) for the respiration=breathing misconception; this is an internal catalog link, dropped from learner-facing guidance.

The pea investigation assumes measurable warming over a day in sealed vacuum flasks; actual temperature rise depends on pea mass, germination vigour and insulation, so treat observed magnitudes as condition-dependent rather than guaranteed.

Activity 1 cites the NGSS PS3.D claim, which supports the respiration chemistry the model represents (oxygen in, CO2/water out, stored energy released) but not the comparative efficacy of a driveable model; the modelling design remains an unvalidated proposal and the medium claim is not evidenced by any source.

assess.poeTask: Set up two sealed vacuum flasks each with a temperature probe: one holding living germinating peas, one holding peas that have been boiled (dead) then cooled. Before revealing anything, ask the child to predict which flask (if either) will warm up over a day, and WHY. The pre-observation reason is the diagnostic part: a child who thinks respiration needs exercise or breathing predicts no change; a child with the cellular idea predicts the living peas warm up because respiration releases energy even in still, non-breathing organisms.
probeDeeper: You said she breathes faster when she runs — what is that extra breathing actually FOR; what do the muscle cells need more of?
Does a potato left in a dark cupboard respire? How could you tell?
If she held her breath for a while, do her cells stop respiring immediately, or is something else going on?
Where exactly in the cell does aerobic respiration take place, and why does that location matter?
assess.correctAnswer: Yes — respiration happens in every living cell all the time, releasing energy from glucose using oxygen (glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water) to keep the body working even at rest; it is not the same as breathing and does not switch off when she stops exercising.

errorPatterns.pattern: respiration is the same as breathing ('respiring just means taking breaths in and out')
errorPatterns.nextMove: separate the words explicitly: breathing = the physical movement of air; respiration = the chemical release of energy inside every cell; show a leaf cell respires though it has no lungs
errorPatterns.revealedBy: in the reason tier justifies 'yes' with 'because she's still breathing', or uses the two words interchangeably

errorPatterns.pattern: respiration only happens during exercise ('you only respire when you run, that's why you puff')
errorPatterns.nextMove: point out the heart still beats and the brain still works at rest, all needing energy from respiration; exercise raises the RATE, it does not switch respiration on
errorPatterns.revealedBy: answers 'no' on the grounds that she is resting

errorPatterns.pattern: only animals respire; plants photosynthesise instead of respiring
errorPatterns.nextMove: establish respiration is universal to living cells, plant and animal; plants both photosynthesise AND respire
errorPatterns.revealedBy: surfaces on the probe when asked whether a plant respires

errorPatterns.nextMove: reframe as releasing stored chemical energy from glucose, not creating energy from nothing
errorPatterns.revealedBy: says respiration produces/creates energy rather than releasing it from glucose

responseLevels.gap: Equates respiration with breathing, or says respiration only happens during exercise; cannot write the word equation.
responseLevels.full: Explains respiration as continuous energy release in every cell's mitochondria, distinct from breathing, and relates raised breathing/heart rate during exercise to greater oxygen and glucose demand — transferring the idea to a resting body or a plant.
responseLevels.partial: Writes glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water and knows it releases energy, but lists these as separate facts — cannot connect why breathing and heart rate rise during exercise to the cells' increased oxygen/glucose demand, or cannot state that respiration is continuous and cellular.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A footballer sits completely still on the bench, not moving at all. Are the cells in her body still respiring right now? Say yes or no — and tell me how you know.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who confuses respiration with breathing, or thinks respiration only happens during exercise, answers 'no, she's resting' or 'only when she runs'; a child holding the cellular idea says yes and separates the constant cellular process from the raised breathing rate that exercise demands. The reason tier is essential because both types could guess 'yes'.
